llm_brief.text:
On the table: the request, quoted: "a recipe for mammoth steak", with mammoth read two ways, the extinct animal or very large. The record of mammoth meat is survival and scavenging, not a cooking tradition: frozen carcasses keep their meat, dogs and wild animals eat it, one frying attempt failed, and a lab mammoth meatball exists that no one has tasted. Buyable stand-ins are horse, reindeer, moose and bison; elephant is restricted. Thaw: a frozen cut thaws in the fridge at 40 F or below, about 24 hours per 4 to 5 lb, so a large cut starts days before the salt lead. Cook numbers (illustrative): a reverse sear at 225 to 275 F for 45 to 120 minutes on a 2 inch cut, a sear then oven at 350 to 450 F, 4 to 6 minutes a side at 2 inches, the core rising 5 to 10 F on a steak and 10 to 15 F on a roast while it rests. Deep cuts: steppe bison, aurochs, khorkhog (mutton cooked with hot stones in a sealed pot), Yakutsk horse steak seared two minutes in a dry cast iron skillet.
Ways in: the show plate, bone-in and carved at the table; the even slab at scale, the same method stretched with thickness setting the timing; the game cut, mellowed by salt lead, fat and aromatics; the ice-age table, mammoth as story with the leftovers planned.
Dials: salt lead time, from 1 to 2 hours for a thin steak by the rule of thumb to 12 to 48 for a roast, about 1/2 tsp kosher per pound; core target, rare 120 to 125 F, medium-rare 130 to 135, medium 140 to 145, medium-well 150 to 155, each with the texture it gives; heat route, low first for an even band, high first for the crust, coals for the edge; thickness, 1 inch to 2 inches and beyond, each changing the lag and the lead; bone-in size, about 2 to 3 inches for a tomahawk or 3 inches and more for a roast-sized cut that overhangs the platter.
Worn paths: the usual move is "salt to taste" or "until golden"; fresher: salt in grams or percent of weight, time in minutes, and the core temperature beside each step. The usual move is "mammoth steak is impossible" and stopping at extinction; fresher: name the buyable stand-in and its recipe, or cook the huge-slab reading at beef scale. The usual move is "carve straight off the heat"; fresher: a long, loose rest, then carving across the grain or at the table. A low core after the rest is often answered by a rack in a low oven until it reads target, then a brief sear (inferred); a wide grey band already present has no fetched fix, and a short sear limits it. The usual move is hype such as "perfect" or "game-changing"; fresher: the number and the texture that make the point.
Open: head count is not stated; the technical default is 4 adults, and portion weight runs on the ss-crowd-scale spread (about 0.5 to 0.75 lb cooked per adult). Oven or grill, cuisine, and whether mammoth is meant literally are left open, with each reading kept.

request._about: The user's words, verbatim from the prompt. Nothing glossed.

up-recipe.text: The deliverable is a recipe: a cooking procedure for a steak called mammoth steak.

up-mammoth.text: The word mammoth names the steak. It carries both the extinct animal and the sense of very large.

primer._about: Research answers for the gap round: food safety and salt by weight (primer rung).

rp-maillard.text: Browning needs a dry surface; a wet surface steams gray until its water has evaporated.
behaviors: A damp steak steams and greys before it browns
Patting dry with paper towel is the usual fix
rp-maillard.principle: Surface water must boil off before the surface can climb into browning temperatures.
signals: gray band instead of brown crust

rp-carryover.term: heat transfer and carry-over in thick cuts
rp-carryover.text: The exterior of a thick cut stays hotter than its center, so the center keeps rising after it leaves the heat.
behaviors: A larger cut rises further while it rests
A hotter oven leaves more heat in the surface to pass inward
rp-carryover.principle: Pull the cut before the target, since the core keeps climbing until the temperature evens out.

rp-food-safety.term: food safety for whole-muscle and large cuts
rp-food-safety.text: Whole-muscle steak is surface-contaminated, so searing the outside is the key step; large cuts need a probed core.
behaviors: A large cut is safe at its core only when the probe reads the target there, not at the surface
rp-food-safety.principle: Whole-muscle safety rests on the surface and the core reading, not on time alone.
signals: leftovers refrigerated within about two hours

rp-recipe-writing.term: how a recipe states quantities, sizes, times and temperatures
rp-recipe-writing.text: A recipe states weight beside volume, thickness beside weight, time as a range, and temperature in F with C beside it.
behaviors: A size given as thickness and weight lets a cook check the cut before cooking
rp-recipe-writing.principle: Give the cook a number to check against, plus the cue that confirms it.

rp-food-safety-game.term: minimum internal temperature for whole-muscle and game meat
rp-food-safety-game.text: Sources give 145 F for intact whole-muscle meat, including commercially raised game, but 160 F for venison; the sources disagree and the dump does not pick one.
behaviors: An intact steak or roast of commercially raised game reaches 145 F under the state rule
Venison in the Penn State guidance reaches 160 F, jerky included
Ground meat sits in the 155 F tier of the same rule table; the fetched text does not label which food that row covers
rp-food-safety-game.principle: Whole-muscle game has a lower sourced threshold than venison; the venison line is the stricter published one.
signals: probe reads 145 F in the thickest part
conflicts: Penn State Extension: 160 F for venison
WA WAC 246-215-03400: 145 F for intact meat including game commercially raised for food
USDA beef chart: not fetched this session (robots block and empty archive), so no quoted USDA figure

rp-kosher-salt-weight.term: kosher salt by weight and brand
rp-kosher-salt-weight.text: A teaspoon of Morton kosher salt weighs about 1.7 times a teaspoon of Diamond Crystal, so half a teaspoon per pound lands at 0.31 to 0.53 percent of meat weight by brand.
behaviors: Half a teaspoon of Diamond Crystal per pound is about 1.4 g, about 0.31 percent of the meat
Half a teaspoon of Morton per pound is about 2.4 g, about 0.53 percent
The amazingribs rule names only kosher salt; its photo caption names Morton, so the 0.53 end is the one the page shows
rp-kosher-salt-weight.principle: Volume measures disagree by brand, so weight is the portable unit; the percent is arithmetic on the sourced grams.
signals: salt weighed, not spooned, for brines

rp-dry-brine.term: salting and dry brining by thickness
rp-dry-brine.text: Salt sprinkled ahead and left uncovered draws moisture out, then the brine returns into the meat.
behaviors: A thicker cut needs the salt to start earlier
Salt pulls moisture out, then reabsorbs it with the salt
The 1 to 2 hour figure matches the under-1-inch note, so it describes thin steaks
A 2-inch steak's 12 to 24 hours is an interpolation between the thin-cut hours and the roast range, not a sourced figure
rp-dry-brine.principle: Salt needs time to move from the surface toward the center; thickness sets how much time.

sourcing_and_cut._about: Outside facts for buying and thawing game-style meat, each labelled with its source. Stand-in channels, the elephant rule and the thaw time come from fetched pages; store types marked inferred come from search snippets only.

readings._about: Readings of the request, side by side. None is chosen for the consumer.

includes: real or analogue game meat framed as mammoth
source, season, cook, rest, carve, serve
sc-read-literal.text: Cook a large game cut framed as mammoth, with a named buyable analogue for the shopping step. This covers the whole job.

sc-read-beef.text: Read mammoth as very large. A huge slab of ordinary beef, cooked by the same method at larger scale.

sc-read-frame.text: Mammoth is the frame for a recipe: presentation and story carry the name, and the cut can be any large steak.

sc-read-analogue.text: Use a named analogue as the actual meat, with the mammoth name carried by framing. Elephant is restricted; bison is the common game option.

decisions._about: Decision points with their tradeoffs. The consumer chooses.

sc-dp-meat.text: Real mammoth has no buyable source. An analogue is shoppable but changes flavor and the story.

sc-dp-bone.text: Bone-in gives the tomahawk shape and show; boneless gives an even slab and simpler carving.

sc-dp-thickness.text: Thickness sets cook time, salt lead time and carry-over; a 2 inch slab needs the longest lead.

options._about: options, not requirements: sourcing and cut options where nothing decides them

sc-opt-literal.text: Name a horse, reindeer or bison analogue in the shopping step, and carry mammoth as the story.

sc-opt-beef.text: Buy a 2 inch bone-in tomahawk from a butcher and frame it as mammoth.

sc-opt-whimsy.text: Serve whole for a show, or carve thick slices across the grain.

rs-bison-channels.text: Bison sells online as whole steaks and roasts, and as ground. US ranches ship nationwide; a Canadian retailer sells flash-frozen packs.
properties: named whole cuts: ribeye, strip, tenderloin
behaviors: A named ribeye or tenderloin in the listing means a whole steak can be ordered directly
Frozen packs keep for a later thaw, which sets the timing

rs-reindeer-channels.text: Reindeer is sold as whole fillet and tenderloin by a Swedish online game butcher, which offers frozen game meat year round.
behaviors: Fillet and tenderloin are whole cuts, so reindeer can stand in for a steak
Ships frozen, so a thaw step applies

rs-horse-channels.text: Lead from a search snippet, not fetched text: specialty butchers serving ethnic or game meat, and online sellers in several countries, with import and legality checks needed first.
properties: online seller (check shipping and import rules)
behaviors: Availability is uneven in Western supermarkets, so a specialty butcher is the likelier first stop
signals: horse steak in a butcher case
horse on an ethnic market shelf

rs-elephant-rule.text: In the US, African elephant ivory is restricted under the ESA rule. Other parts and products are allowed with the permits named in 50 CFR parts 13, 14 and 23.
behaviors: Meat is not barred outright under this rule, so a sale still needs the permits
The rule covers US commerce; other countries and CITES were not checked

rs-mammoth-no-source.text: No fetched source names a legal sale of mammoth meat, nor forbids one. The no-buyable-source claim rests on the species' extinction and the thin eating record in rs-mammoth-finds.
rs-mammoth-no-source.principle: Absence in fetched sources is not proof of a rule; the claim stays inferred.

sc-thaw.term: refrigerator thaw for a frozen cut
sc-thaw.rung: large-cut and game-meat cookery (thaw before the salt lead)
sc-thaw.text: Refrigerator thawing takes about 24 hours per 4 to 5 pounds, held at 40 F or below. Converted, that is about 10 to 13 hours per kilogram (inferred). No fetched source gives a per-inch time.
behaviors: A 15 lb cut takes about three days, so the thaw starts before the salt lead
A 4 to 5 lb cut needs about a day in the fridge before salting
sc-thaw.principle: Thaw time scales with mass; food-safety guidance keeps the thaw cold the whole time.

rs-mammoth-finds.text: Permafrost mammoth carcasses survive with meat intact, but documented eating is thin: dogs and wild animals eat the frozen meat, and one researcher's frying attempt failed.
behaviors: Frozen meat is eaten by dogs and wild animals, per the KTH account
Frying old meat turned it to a strange liquid, per the same researcher
KTH calls the meat a nutritious source of protein for dogs, but says humans face a different story
rs-mammoth-finds.principle: The record shows survival and scavenging, not a cooking tradition.

rs-mammoth-debate.text: Pleistocene Park's leaders say large herbivores help compact snow over permafrost, and say modern animals can do that job without mammoths. Critics call de-extinction a pretext.
behaviors: Debate sources are general coverage, not meat reports
rs-mammoth-debate.principle: Cited from search snippets only; no fetched page confirms these views.

rs-analogues.term: analogues eaten in Yakutia, and a lab mammoth meatball
rs-analogues.text: Closest real eating comes from Yakutia's horse and reindeer; a lab-grown mammoth meatball exists, and no one has tasted it.
behaviors: Yakutsk restaurant cook: a horse steak, no seasoning, two minutes in a bone-dry cast iron skillet
Vow grew the mammoth gene in a sheep cell, so the product is not mammoth tissue
rs-analogues.principle: Real game analogues to a mammoth are horse, reindeer, moose and bison, each sold through different channels.

rs-analogue-limits.term: legal and practical limits on analogues
rs-analogue-limits.text: Elephant meat is the hardest analogue to source in the US: ivory trade is near-total banned, and no fetched source confirmed the meat rules.
behaviors: Elephant meat legality is unresolved in this research; check the Fish and Wildlife rules before sourcing
Bison is the mildest game meat of the common options, per one snippet
rs-analogue-limits.principle: Snippet-level facts only; confirm against federal wildlife rules (50 CFR Part 23) before relying on them.

rs-tomahawk-size.text: A tomahawk is about two inches thick with a bone up to a foot or longer; the rib meat weighs about two pounds.
properties: two to three inches thick around bone
about two pounds of rib steak
behaviors: Bone length varies with how the butcher cuts it, per the Chicago guide
Larger animals give more meat and longer rib bones
rs-tomahawk-size.principle: The bone adds length, not thickness: the meat around it sets the slab's depth.

rs-butcher-weights.term: weight to thickness for butcher cuts
rs-butcher-weights.text: Boneless ribeye thickness tracks weight roughly: about 1 inch at 12 oz, 1.5 inches at 14 to 16 oz. A standard retail ribeye is about 1.25 inches.
behaviors: A 2-inch slab reads as roast-sized at crowd portions
Ask the butcher for target weight and thickness
Thicker cuts need salt and carry-over planning
rs-butcher-weights.principle: From one search snippet; the ranges are spreads, not a cut standard.

rs-horse-region.term: horse meat as a staple protein
rs-horse-region.text: Horse is eaten as everyday protein in Yakutia (Sakha, Eastern Siberia), alongside reindeer and moose. The article is about Yakutsk food.
behaviors: Horse is a regional protein, not a supermarket staple in most countries

cook_and_doneness._about: Gap-round answers for heat route, sear, dry brine and recovery. Spreads, with the sources' disagreements kept.

cd-heat-route.term: reverse sear, sear then oven, grill
cd-heat-route.text: Three heat routes for a thick cut, each leaving a different grey band and a different time near target.
behaviors: Reverse sear at 225 to 275 F until the core is 10 to 15 F under target, then a 1 to 2 minute sear a side leaves an even band edge to edge
Sear then oven at 350 to 450 F gives a short crust time but a thicker grey band on a thick cut
Grill over coals runs hotter at the surface, so the edge can overcook on a 2 inch cut before the centre rises
cd-heat-route.principle: Low heat first gives an even band from edge to centre; high heat first builds the crust before the core moves.
signals: even pink from edge to edge
thin grey ring under the crust

cd-dry-brine.text: Salt goes on early and uncovered; lead time grows with thickness, and the surface looks wet for a while.
behaviors: A 1 inch cut salted 45 minutes to overnight seasons toward the middle
A 2 inch cut salted 12 to 24 hours carries salt to the centre
A roast-sized cut salted 12 to 48 hours; pat the surface dry before searing
cd-dry-brine.principle: Salt moves inward slowly, so the lead time is the distance it must travel.
signals: seasoning through the middle when sliced
dry surface just before the sear

cd-rest-carryover.text: The centre keeps climbing after the cut leaves the heat, so pull before the target and rest before carving.
behaviors: A 1.5 inch steak climbs about 5 to 10 F while it rests
A roast-sized cut climbs 10 to 15 F and rests longer, about 15 to 30 minutes
Carving straight off the heat lets the juices run that a rest would have kept
cd-rest-carryover.principle: Heat in the outside keeps moving inward, so the target is reached on the rest, not on the heat.

cd-large-cut-heat.term: large-cut heat transfer and fat cap
cd-large-cut-heat.text: A huge cut lags: the centre takes far longer to rise than the surface takes to brown, and the fat cap renders on its own schedule.
behaviors: A 2 inch cut takes roughly two to four times as long as a 1 inch cut to bring the centre to target
Rendering the fat cap edge-on for 3 to 6 minutes melts it before the meat crust forms
A thick fat cap can need several more minutes, so render until it is clear and crisp
cd-large-cut-heat.principle: Surface heat moves inward slowly, so the thicker the cut, the more of the cook happens after the surface looks done.
signals: surface brown while the centre is cold

cd-thick-mistakes.text: Frequent misses with thick steaks: a damp surface, one probe read, carving too early, and a cold centre under a fast sear.
behaviors: A damp surface steams for the first minute and greys the crust
A probe in the surface reads hotter than the centre
A cold centre under a fast sear leaves the edge overcooked before the middle is warm
cd-thick-mistakes.principle: Most misses come from a surface reading taken as the core reading, or from time the cut needed and did not get.
signals: grey edge with a raw centre

cd-recovery.term: recovery for a low core or a wide grey band
cd-recovery.text: Sources give prevention rather than repair: the grey band forms during browning, and no fetched source says how to fix a steak already cooked.
behaviors: Prevention: warm to 95 F in a 275 F oven, then sear just before serving (ATK)
A low core after the rest: back on a rack in a low oven until it reads target, then rest and a brief sear (inferred from the ATK warm step)
A wide grey band already present: no fetched fix; a short sear limits further widening (inferred)
A roast is taken off within 10 F of target and rested, so a low core is rarely a carry-over problem (roast source)
cd-recovery.principle: The band is made during browning, so repair only thins it; the probe reading, not time, says when the core is done.
signals: core still under target after rest
grey ring thicker than a fingertip
conflicts: ATK's pan-roast to 450 F gave a wide band; its 275 F warm-up gave a rosy interior

cd-doneness.text: Doneness is a target core temperature; the published safety threshold for whole muscle is a separate number.
behaviors: Pulling at 125 F gives a rare centre that settles near 130 F after the rest
Medium-rare sits below the 145 F whole-muscle figure; some cooks accept that as a taste choice and others follow the minimum, so the recipe can state which
The 145 F USDA whole-muscle figure is build knowledge, not a fetched quote; verify before the recipe quotes it
cd-doneness.principle: Pick the core target from the texture wanted; the safety threshold is a separate, published figure.

cd-sear.text: Sear on a hot, dry surface; the crust forms in the first minutes, so the time follows the browning and the core target.
properties: cast iron or heavy steel pan
behaviors: A 1 to 1.5 inch cut browns in 2 to 4 minutes a side with one turn or several; a single turn holds the crust steadier, and frequent flips brown more slowly
A 2 inch cut takes 4 to 6 minutes a side at a slightly lower heat so the outside browns before the centre overshoots
Turning every 30 to 60 seconds browns more slowly but cools the surface less per flip
cd-sear.principle: Browning needs a hot, dry surface; the thickness sets how far the heat must travel to the centre.
signals: deep brown crust with no gray band

cd-reverse-sear-pull.term: reverse sear pull point and oven setting
cd-reverse-sear-pull.text: Oven 200 to 275 F; pull 8 to 15 F under the final target before the sear, and the rest and sear carry the centre the rest of the way.
behaviors: Pull 8 F under: a blog table pulls medium-rare at 112 F for a 130 F finish, though its text says 8 F under
Pull 10 to 15 F under: about 115 F for a 125 to 130 F finish, from a blog that sears about a minute a side
A bigger cut climbs more on rest, so the pull sits lower in the spread
Without a sear, a roast is pulled within 10 F of target and the rest carries it (roast source, not steak)
No fetched source gives a 3-inch oven time; the probe, not the clock, decides
cd-reverse-sear-pull.principle: Pull low enough that the sear and rest carry the centre to target; the spread is the sources' disagreement.
signals: core 8 to 15 F under target at pull

cd-sear-thick.term: sear time per side after a low oven
cd-sear-thick.text: After a low oven, sources give 30 to 60 seconds a side in a smoking pan; a straight sear of a cold thick steak takes minutes, and the band beneath overcooks meanwhile.
behaviors: Finishing a reverse-seared steak: 30 to 60 seconds a side, then the edges
From a warmed centre, the ATK crust forms in under 4 minutes total
A cold thick steak in a hot pan can take upward of 4 minutes a side, and the meat under the surface overcooks
No fetched source gives a 3-inch cast-iron sear time; a single unfetched blog suggests 2 minutes a side over 2 inches
cd-sear-thick.principle: The sear only browns; the thickness is handled by the oven phase, so a long sear on a thick cut widens the band.
signals: deep brown crust with a thin grey ring
wide grey band after a long sear

serving_and_sides._about: Carving, equipment, scaling and gamey-flavor methods are the build's reasoning on the primer facts (inferred). Seasoning and side pools live under options: proposed choices, not requirements.

options._about: options, not requirements: builder choices where the prompt and evidence are silent

ss-season-options.text: Each seasoning shapes the crust and the first bite differently; pick one or layer two.
behaviors: Salt only keeps the meat's own taste most present
Pepper and garlic burn at high sear heat, so add them late or to a cooler finish
Herb butter melts over the rested cut and adds the fat that mellows game
Smoke adds a layer but needs a long low cook or a smoker, which changes timing
A juniper, red wine or vinegar marinade suits a gamey cut
ss-season-options.principle: Seasoning chooses what sits on the crust and what the first bite tastes of.

ss-side-options.term: sides for a big red meat
ss-side-options.text: Sides that cut through the richness, or that soak up the pan juices.
properties: large tray of roast roots for a show
behaviors: Acid pickles and horseradish cut the fat of a rich cut
Potatoes and bread soak up the juices from the rest
Charred greens add bitterness that balances the sweet crust
ss-side-options.principle: Richness is balanced by acid, bitterness or starch; a huge cut calls for sides that stretch.

ss-carve.term: carving a thick steak across the grain
ss-carve.text: Rest the cut, then slice across the grain into even pieces so each bite has short fibers.
behaviors: Cutting before the rest lets juice run onto the board
Slices of a thick cut show the full band from crust to center
ss-carve.principle: Short cut fibers chew tender, and slicing after the rest keeps the juice in the meat.
signals: grain running one direction on each slice

ss-gamey-mellow.text: Gamey taste sits in fat and surface; trimming, salting, soaking, basting and aromatics change what the palate reads.
behaviors: Trimming removes the fat where much of the gamey taste sits
An acid marinade works on the outside only, so it adds brightness, not depth
A milk soak adds a day of lead time and a rinse and dry step before searing
A long acid soak can leave the surface soft
ss-gamey-mellow.principle: Each method changes a different layer: fat, surface, or the aromatics on top.
signals: strong gamey smell on the raw cut

ss-equipment.text: A probe thermometer decides doneness; the pan, sheet and grill set the crust and the finish.
behaviors: A probe in the thickest part confirms the core before carving
A dry cast-iron pan gives a fast hard sear, as the Yakutsk cook used for horse
A wire rack on a sheet pan lets air reach the underside for the oven finish
ss-equipment.principle: The heat source sets the crust; the probe sets when the cut is done.

ss-quantities.term: pan fat, butter and aromatics per pound
ss-quantities.text: Pan oil and butter are amounts per pound: a thin oil coat for the sear, then a butter baste at the end for the richer finish. Illustrative, not sourced.
properties: add late for a high sear
behaviors: A thin coat of oil, about 1 tsp per lb, sears clean; more pools and spatters at high heat
A butter baste of 1 to 2 tbsp per lb over the last minute or two gives a richer finish and browns the crust
ss-quantities.principle: Quantity sets how much fat reaches the crust; the butter sets the finish, and it goes in late so it browns rather than burns.
signals: thin dark crust with no pooled oil
butter foaming and browning over the last minute

tokens.butter_tbsp_per_lb_finish: 1 to 2, basted in the last 1 to 2 minutes

ss-aromatics.term: pepper, garlic and herbs per pound
ss-aromatics.text: Pepper, garlic and herbs are amounts per pound, each a spread; when each goes in sets whether it toasts or burns. Illustrative, not sourced.
properties: add late for a high sear
behaviors: Coarse pepper at 1 to 2 tsp per lb forms the crust; it scorches if it goes in before a long high sear, so add it late
Garlic at 2 to 4 cloves per lb in the butter perfumes the finish without burning when added in the last minute
Herbs at 1 to 2 tbsp per lb stirred into the butter melt over the rested cut; the same herbs in a hot dry pan go black
ss-aromatics.principle: Quantity sets how much seasoning reaches the crust, and when it goes in sets whether it toasts or burns.
signals: thin dark crust with no pooled oil
butter foaming and browning over the last minute

tokens.pepper_tsp_per_lb_coarse: 1 to 2 for a crust; 2 to 3 for a heavy crust
tokens.garlic_cloves_per_lb: 2 to 4 in the butter; 4 to 6 for a garlic-forward finish
tokens.herb_tbsp_per_lb: 1 to 2 chopped, stirred into the butter

ss-crowd-scale.text: Scale by cooked meat per person and by how many cuts; time follows thickness and weight, not headcount. Raw weight to buy runs higher, since cooking loses weight.
behaviors: One huge cut takes longer than several cuts of the same thickness
Two cuts of equal thickness cook in about the time one takes, if the pan holds both
Cooking loses about 20 to 30 percent of raw weight, so raw purchase runs about a quarter above the cooked target
A smaller portion (200 to 300 g, the ak-one-serving reading) needs fewer pounds and can fit one cut; 12 oz cooked each pushes toward a larger single cut or more cuts
ss-crowd-scale.principle: Heat reaches the center by thickness; headcount only sets how much meat to buy.
signals: cut weight written beside people served
raw weight on the label, cooked weight on the plate

tokens.shrink_cooked_fraction: 0.70 to 0.80 (20 to 30 percent lost in cooking)
tokens.cut_options_total_raw_lb: 2 to 3 cuts of 1.5 to 2 lb: 3 to 6; one 4 to 6 lb cut: 4 to 6; 3 cuts of 2.5 to 3 lb: 7.5 to 9; one 8 to 10 lb cut: 8 to 10; 4 cuts of 3 to 3.5 lb: 12 to 14

lexicon._about: Vocabulary and associations around mammoth steak. Seed material at tier 2 to 4, inferred; it widens the request and never defines it. Deep cuts are marked.

lx-mammoth-quality.text: The adjective sense of mammoth: the steak is meant to be enormous, each reading at full strength.

readings.in_practice: Two inches or more thick, bone-in, roast-sized. It overhangs the platter, needs its own pan or grate, and is checked with a probe.
readings.exemplar: a tomahawk over the grill, two inches thick, probe-checked (illustrative)

readings.reading: prehistoric or mythic feel carried by name and presentation
readings.in_practice: Served on slate or a bone-shaped board, fire lit in the dining room, an ice-age story on the menu. Full strength: a relic served as a relic.
readings.exemplar: a slate board, candles lit, and an ice-age line on the menu (illustrative)

readings.in_practice: Carved by the host into slabs for the whole party, platters refilled. Full strength: more meat than anyone can eat, leftovers planned as a second meal.
readings.exemplar: a host carving one big roast into slabs for eight at one table (illustrative)

readings.in_practice: A boneless, even slab as wide as the platter and an inch or more thick, cut across the grain from a whole muscle. Full strength: one piece that overhangs both plates and is carved at the table.
readings.exemplar: a whole top sirloin cap cut into one thick, platter-wide slab (illustrative)

readings.reading: bone-in roast-sized cut, cooked and carved as a roast
readings.in_practice: A bone-in section three inches or more thick, cooked and carved as a roast rather than a steak: the bone runs past the plate and sets the length, the roast sets the time. Full strength: a bone that needs its own cutting board.
readings.exemplar: a bone-in rib section roasted whole and carved at the table (illustrative)

lx-mammoth-descriptors.term: how people describe a huge cut
lx-mammoth-descriptors.text: Words people reach for when a cut is enormous. They name size, age and weight before flavor.
metaphors: a slab that carries the table

lx-adjacent-concepts.text: Things near a mammoth in time, place and cooking. The deep cuts are the less obvious half.
deep_cuts: khorkhog, mutton cooked with hot stones in a sealed pot

lx-kw-technical.text: Terms a cookbook or meat-science text would use for a huge cut.

lx-kw-sensory-mood.text: How the cooked cut tastes, feels and sets the room. Sensory words describe the plate; mood words describe the table.

lx-search-queries.text: Phrases people type, grouped in this order: recipe, animal, technique and crowd.
queries: thick steak dry brine how many days
steak internal temperature medium rare chart
how much steak per person bone-in

rs-game-vocab.text: Gamey is a catchall, not a single sensory attribute; meat scientists tie it to red colour, fat and toughness, and to overcooking.
behaviors: Darker, redder muscle reads gamier
Overcooking brings out latent gamey notes, so lean game dries and turns stronger
Some consumers read gamey as wild authenticity; others count it a fault
rs-game-vocab.principle: Fat carries most of the wild flavor; lean meat shows it plainly.

rs-huge-cut-words.text: Huge bone-in rib steaks go by tomahawk, cowboy steak, tomahawk ribeye or bone-in ribeye.
behaviors: The name carries the bone shape; the meat is the same as a ribeye

lx-influences.text: Cooking traditions that handle huge cuts. Each one contributes a method or a presentation; none is a style to copy.
contribution: Argentine asado: wood embers, a slow pace, the grill as the social centre
Brazilian churrasco: coarse salt as the seasoning, meat on skewers, carving at the table
Florentine bistecca alla fiorentina: a thick bone-in cut, traditionally served rare, little seasoning
Texas barbecue: long smoke, fat rendered into the bark, brisket as the big-format benchmark
Chicago steakhouse tomahawk: the bone as spectacle, a cut sized for a table
Mongolian khorkhog: hot stones in a sealed pot, slow and even heat, mutton
Yakutian cold-climate eating: unseasoned horse steak seared fast in a dry cast-iron pan
